links.note: 1281 says that rejoicing at a thought (உள்ளக் களித்தல்) and delight at a sight (காண மகிழ்தல்) belong to love and not to liquor (கள்ளுக்கில்). 1090 makes the sight half of this claim at the very start of the Book of Love: brewed liquor gladdens only those who drink it (உண்டார்கண் அல்லது), not, as love does, those who merely see (கண்டார் மகிழ்செய்தல் இன்று). The comparison that opens the courtship returns here after the separation, now with thought added to sight.

1201 says love is sweeter than liquor because even thinking of it gives great joy (உள்ளினும் தீராப் பெருமகிழ்... கள்ளினும் காமம் இனிது); 1281 says joy at a thought and at a sight is found in love and not in liquor. Together with 1090 (sight) the three verses form one argument, and 1281 joins the two halves; Parimelazhagar gives 1201 to the man and 1281 to the woman, so both lovers make the claim.

In 1281 love is set above liquor: it delights at a thought and a look, which liquor cannot do. In 1288, in the same chapter, his chest is itself like liquor to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), wanted though it does shameful harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா செயினும்). The chapter uses the one image both ways, first to say love exceeds drink and then to say it compels like drink.

104 says that those who understand its fruit take a help the size of a millet (தினைத்துணை) as the size of a palmyra (பனைத்துணை); 1282 says that when love comes filling to a palmyra's measure there should be no sulking even of a millet's measure. The same millet-and-palmyra pair of measures serves gratitude in one verse and love in the other, in each case to say that a large thing should not be weighed against a small one.

433 says those ashamed of blame treat a fault as small as a millet as if it were a palmyra (தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம்... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்). 1282 uses the same two measures in the other direction: with love as large as a palmyra, even a millet of sulking over his fault is to be avoided. In 433 the small fault is magnified; in 1282 the small grievance is to be dropped.

1302 says sulking is like salt in the right amount and is spoiled only by being prolonged a little (உப்பமைந் தற்றால் புலவி). 1282 says that when love is full to a palmyra's measure, not even a millet of sulking is wanted (தினைத்துணையும் ஊடாமை வேண்டும்). Read together, 1282 states a condition, காமம் நிறைய வரின், under which the measured sulk that 1302 recommends falls to nothing; Parimelazhagar takes 1282 as the woman voicing her own haste in the form of general advice.

1178 ends காணாது அமைவில கண் and 1283 ends காணா தமையல கண்: in both her eyes cannot rest without seeing a man who desires without cherishing (பேணாது பெட்டார் in 1178, பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும் in 1283). 1178 is spoken in his absence and 1283 on his return, so the pair shows the same complaint about her eyes holding on both sides of the separation.

1257 says she knows nothing of shame when the one she cherishes does, in desire, what she wants (பேணியார் பெட்ப செயின்). 1283 reuses the two words with the sense turned round: even if he does only what he himself wants, without cherishing her (பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்), her eyes will not rest without seeing him. The second verse removes the condition of the first: her yielding does not depend on his doing what pleases her.

1259: she went away saying she would sulk (புலப்பல் எனச் சென்றேன்) and embraced him on seeing her heart begin to join with him. 1284: she went to sulk (ஊடற்கண் சென்றேன்) and her heart, forgetting that, went to unite (கூடற்கண் சென்றது). The two verses report the same event in the same sentence shape, in 1259 as a failure of her restraint (the chapter is நிறையழிதல்) and in 1284 as eagerness for union.

1246 tells the heart that when it sees the lover it cannot stay in a sulk, so its present anger is false (பொய்க்காய்வு). 1284 is that prediction coming true: she set out to sulk and the heart forgot it and went to unite (அதுமறந்து கூடற்கண் சென்றது).

1284 reports to her friend that her heart forgot the sulk and went to unite. 1294 gives the consequence: since the heart will not first sulk and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), who will consult with it about such things again (நின்னொடு சூழ்வார் யார்). The report of the heart's desertion in one chapter becomes the quarrel with the heart in the next.

1127: because her lover lives in her eyes she will not even line them with kohl (கண்ணும் எழுதேம்), knowing he would be hidden. 1285: as the eye cannot see the kohl-stick at the moment of lining (எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்), she cannot see his fault when she sees him. Both build on the lining of the eye, once for his constant presence in her sight and once for her blindness to his fault when he is near.

1285 gives the image: the eye does not see the stick that is lining it, and she does not see his blame when she sees him (பழிகாணேன் கண்ட இடத்து). 1286 states the other half that the image implies: when she does not see him she sees nothing but his faults (காணாக்கால் காணேன் தவறல்லவை). Parimelazhagar's gloss on 1285 already supplies this, saying the eye has seen the stick at every other time.

190 asks what harm could come if people saw their own faults as they see strangers' faults (ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்). 1285 says she cannot see her husband's fault when he is before her, as the eye cannot see the kohl-stick touching it. In both, what is nearest is what goes unseen; 190 treats this as a failing to correct, and 1285 as a fact about love.

1286: seeing him, she sees no faults; not seeing him, she sees nothing else. In 1297 she calls her heart மடநெஞ்சு, and Parimelazhagar defines that மடமை as exactly this reversal: remembering when he is absent, and forgetting when he is present, faults that ought to be remembered at sight and forgotten in absence. On his reading 1297 names and blames what 1286 only describes.

1134: the fierce flood of love carries off the raft of shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும்). 1287: why sulk knowing it will prove false, like those who leap into a stream knowing it will carry them off (உய்த்தல் அறிந்து புனல்பாய்பவர்). The same water and the same verb, உய்த்தல், are used by the man of his restraint in 1134 and by the woman of her sulk here.

1260 asks whether those whose hearts are like fat put in fire (நிணந்தீயில் இட்டன்ன) can say they will hold out in a sulk. 1287 asks what use it is to sulk when one knows it will fail (பொய்த்தல் அறிந்தென் புலந்து). Both are rhetorical questions that deny she can keep up a sulk, one by the image of fat melting and one by the image of a current.

1145: as drinking is wanted more each time one gets drunk (களித்தொறும் கள்ளுண்டல் வேட்டற்றால்), love is sweeter each time it is exposed. 1288: his chest is as liquor is to those who have got drunk on it (களித்தார்க்குக் கள்ளற்றே), though it does shameful harm. Both take the drinker's returning appetite as the likeness for love; 1288 adds the harm and the shame that 1145 leaves out.

924 says the good woman called Shame turns her back on those with the great fault of liquor (நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும்). 1288 likens his chest to liquor that does disgraceful harm (இளித்தக்க இன்னா) and is still wanted; Parimelazhagar names the harms as loss of shame and of self-restraint. What Book Two condemns in the drinker the love verse accepts as its own comparison.

940: as the gambler loves the game more with each loss (இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல்), the living being loves life more with each suffering. 1288: liquor is wanted by the drunk even as it does them shameful harm, and so is his chest. Both explain an attachment that grows through injury by a vice from the same group of chapters (dice in 940, liquor in 1288).

90: the anicham withers when merely smelled, and a guest withers when looked at with a changed face. 1289: love is more delicate than a flower (மலரினும் மெல்லிது) and few reach its right moment (செவ்வி). A flower's fragility measures the guest's sensitivity in the household chapters and love's in the Book of Love, and in both the point is how little it takes to spoil the thing. (The edition's text of 90 has a typo in குழையும்.)

1289 says few attain love's செவ்வி, its right moment or condition. 1306 gives a figure for missing it on either side: without துனி and புலவி love is like fruit over-ripe or unripe (கனியும் கருக்காயும் அற்று). Parimelazhagar places 1289 in a sulk that will not yield to appeasement, so the fineness it speaks of is the same fineness of timing that 1306 puts in terms of ripeness.

In 1290 the man recalls that she sulked with her eyes alone (கண்ணின் துனித்தே) and then, more eager for the embrace than he (என்னினும் தான்விதுப் புற்று), gave way. In 1259 she tells it herself: she went off meaning to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart begin to join with him. The same collapse of a sulk is given once from his side and once from hers.

1290 remembers her sulk ending because her eagerness to embrace was greater than his. 1327 states the rule the man later draws: in a lovers' quarrel the one who loses has won, as is seen in the union (ஊடலில் தோற்றவர் வென்றார்). Her giving way in 1290 is a case of the defeat that 1327 counts as victory.

72: the loveless belong wholly to themselves, and the loving belong to others even in their bones (அன்பிலார் எல்லாம் தமக்குரியர்). 1291: his heart is for him (அவர்நெஞ்சு அவர்க்காதல்), so why, heart, are you not for me (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). The woman's complaint is 72's distinction seen from the inside: the one who loves no longer owns her own heart, and the one who does not love keeps his.

1205 asks whether he, who has shut her out of his heart (தம்நெஞ்சத்து எம்மைக் கடிகொண்டார்), is not ashamed to keep entering hers. 1291 asks her own heart why it is not hers when his heart is his. Both rest on the same imbalance of two hearts; 1205 blames him for it and 1291 blames her heart.

1245 asks the heart whether one can give him up as hostile (செற்றார் எனக் கைவிடல் உண்டோ) merely because he does not respond when she draws close (உற்றால் உறாஅதவர்). 1292 uses the same word for him, உறாஅதவர், and reverses the charge: even after seeing that he is not close, the heart goes to him saying he will not be hostile (செறாஅரென). In 1245 she argues the heart out of abandoning him; in 1292 she reproaches it for not being able to.

1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை) is something the lovesick cannot know. 1292 shows it: her heart goes to him (சேறி) though it has seen that he is not attached to her. 1255 gives the general statement and 1292 the instance, addressed to the heart that does the going.

752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing and everyone honours the rich (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1293 has the woman quote the same worldly observation as a saying, கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல், and ask her heart whether that is why it leaves her and follows him. The pairing shows a hard fact from the chapter on wealth being used in the Book of Love as a taunt, with the woman as the ruined one and her heart as the fair-weather friend.

787 defines friendship as turning a friend from ruin and, when ruin comes, sharing the suffering (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பதாம் நட்பு). The saying in 1293, that the ruined have no friends, describes how the world behaves and not what friendship is; by the standard of 787 her heart, which goes after him as it pleases (பெட்டாங்கு அவர்பின் செலல்), has failed as a friend. The woman's question, என்பதோ, shows she is quoting the saying to reproach, not endorsing it.

798 warns against taking the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார் நட்பு). In 1293 the one who deserts in distress is her own heart, which cannot be declined as a friend. The verse turns the advice of the friendship chapters into a predicament with no remedy.

1330 says sulking is the pleasure of love, and the pleasure of sulking is to come together and embrace (ஊடுதல் காமத்திற்கு இன்பம்). 1294 has the woman want exactly that order, first make a quarrel and then enjoy (துனிசெய்து துவ்வாய்), and complain that her heart will not do it. The book's closing statement of how a sulk should work is, in 1294, a plan she cannot carry out.

1260 asks whether those with hearts like fat in fire can say they will hold out in a sulk (புணர்ந்தூடி நிற்பேம் எனல்). 1294 tells the heart that it will not sulk first and enjoy afterwards, so no one will plan such things with it. Both say the intention to sulk cannot survive her own heart; 1294 adds that she will stop consulting it.

1152 says that once his mere look was pleasure, and now union itself holds the misery of fearing separation (பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). 1295 says her heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்), so its grief never ends. The fear inside union that 1152 notes before he leaves is one of the two fears in 1295 after he has come back.

1179: when he does not come her eyes do not sleep, and when he comes they do not sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின்துஞ்சா), so either way they suffer. 1295: the heart fears when it lacks him and fears when it has him (பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின்பிரிவு அஞ்சும்). The same two-sided trap is stated of the eyes in one chapter and of the heart in another; Parimelazhagar explains the eyes' sleeplessness on his coming by the same fear of parting.

1244 tells the heart to take the eyes along, since they are eating her (இவையென்னைத் தின்னும்) in their wish to see him. 1296 says that when she sat alone and thought, her heart was there as if to eat her (என்னைத் தினிய இருந்தது). The image of being eaten by a part of oneself moves from the eyes to the heart, the very one she had been addressing as an ally in 1244.

293: do not lie about what your heart knows, for after the lie your own heart will burn you (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). 1296: thinking alone, she finds her own heart is there to eat her. In both the tormentor is one's own heart and the setting is solitude with what one knows; 293 makes this the working of conscience, and 1296 gives it as the experience of the abandoned lover, with no fault of hers involved.

1207 says she does not know forgetting, and even remembering burns her heart (உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்). 1296 says that when she sits alone and thinks (நினைத்தக்கால்), her heart consumes her. Both make thinking of him in his absence the source of the pain; in 1207 the heart is what is burned, in 1296 it is what does the harm.

1247 tells the heart to give up either desire or shame, since she cannot bear both (காமம் விடுஒன்றோ நாண்விடு). 1297 reports how that ended: caught up with a foolish heart that cannot forget him (அவர்மறக் கல்லா), she has forgotten even shame (நாணும் மறந்தேன்). The choice she put to the heart in 1247 is settled in 1297 by the heart's incapacity, not by her decision.

1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame's sake and do not give up shame for life's sake (நாண்துறவார்). In 1297 the woman has forgotten shame because her heart cannot forget him, and Parimelazhagar glosses the shame as dearer to her than life, the valuation of 1017. The pairing sets the rule from the chapter on shame beside a speaker in the Book of Love who holds that rule and reports failing it; it is her confession, not a contrary teaching.

In 1132 the man says his body and life, unable to bear it, will mount the palmyra horse, with shame set aside (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து). In 1297 the woman says she has forgotten shame through her heart's inability to forget him. Each sex is shown losing நாண் to love; the man sets it aside to act in public, and the woman finds it gone.

1255 says the dignity of not going after one who has turned away is unknown to the lovesick (செற்றார்பின் செல்லாப் பெருந்தகைமை). In 1298 her heart reasons the opposite way about where disgrace lies: it thinks that to scorn him would be a disgrace (எள்ளின் இளிவாம் என்று எண்ணி) and so keeps thinking of his side. 1298 shows the lovesick heart not merely ignorant of that dignity, as 1255 has it, but supplied with its own argument from honour for doing without it.

967 says it is better to be called ruined where one stands than to live by following those who do not accept one (ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின்). In 1298 the heart, described as loving life (உயிர்க்காதல் நெஞ்சு), counts scorning him as the disgrace and goes on dwelling on him. The chapter on honour ranks honour above life; the heart in 1298 keeps the vocabulary of disgrace (இளிவு) but, out of attachment to life, applies it so as to stay with the one who slighted her. This is the heart's reasoning as she reports it, not a rival doctrine.

1184: she thinks of him and what she speaks of is his merit (உரைப்பது அவர்திறம்), and still the pallor comes. 1298: her heart thinks of what pertains to him (அவர்திறம் உள்ளும்), judging that to scorn him would be a disgrace. The phrase அவர் திறம் with உள்ளுதல் appears in both; in 1184 it is her own loyal practice that goes unrewarded, and in 1298 it is something her heart does that she stands apart from.

1299 asks who will be a companion in grief when one's own heart is not (தாமுடைய நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). 1300 repeats the frame, தாமுடைய நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி, and draws the further step: then it is a small matter that strangers are not one's own. The pair moves from the loss of the nearest help to an inference about everyone else, and Parimelazhagar gives both to the man, where the first eight verses of the chapter are the woman's.

1263 describes the man as having left with his own heart or resolve for companion (உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்). 1299 asks who can be a companion in grief when one's own heart is no companion (நெஞ்சந் துணையல் வழி). The heart as துணை is what he had on setting out and, on Parimelazhagar's assignment of 1299 to the man, what he lacks when she will not be reconciled; Manakkudavar gives 1299 to the woman.

36 says virtue, done without delay, is the companion that does not die when one dies (பொன்றுங்கால் பொன்றாத் துணை). 1299 says that in grief there is no companion if one's own heart is not one. Both verses ask what stays with a person when other support is gone; Book One answers virtue, and the lover's verse names the heart and finds it missing.

1291 opens the chapter with the woman asking her heart why it is not hers when his heart is his own (நீ எமக்கு ஆகாதது). 1300 closes it with the general form: when one's own heart is not one's kin (நெஞ்சம் தமரல் வழி), it is nothing that strangers are not. Parimelazhagar gives the first to the woman and the last to the man, so the chapter begins and ends with the same complaint from each side.

188 asks what those who spread even the faults of their closest (துன்னியார்) will do to strangers (ஏதிலார் மாட்டு). 1300 argues that when one's own heart is not one's own, strangers (ஏதிலார்) not being one's own is a slight thing. Both reason from the nearest relation to ஏதிலார்: if the bond fails at the closest point, nothing can be expected further out.

882 says do not fear enemies who are like swords, but fear the tie with enemies who are like kin (கேள்போல் பகைவர்). 1300 finds the same reversal inside one person: the heart that should be தமர், one's own people, is not, and beside that the distance of outsiders hardly counts. The lesson of the chapter on enmity within, that the danger is in what is closest, is applied in 1300 to the heart.
